name: Kéo
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Baird, Louise. 2002. A grammar of Kéo: an Austronesian language of East Nusantara. PhD thesis, Australian National University (hdl 1885/9446).
catalog_locator: sec. 2.6 Stress, p.53 (p.49 of the ANU bitstream 'Baird Thesis ')
catalog_quote: 2.6 Stress. Stress in Indonesian languages is often a controversial issue. However, it is possible to make generalisations. Stress in Kéo is predictable: it typically falls on the penultimate syllable of the word. The exception to this is in disyllabic words in which there is a schwa in the first syllable, in which case stress falls on the ultimate syllable. Primary stress in compounds, as in simple words, falls on the penultimate syllable. Stress in Indonesian loan words also falls on the penultimate syllable. Kéo has one proclitic, the numeral one ~ ha (see §6.4 and §9.2.2). Stress remains on the penultimate syllable in disyllabic words which have the clitic attached to them. The clitic itself is typically unstressed, and is often realised as a schwa.

audit.reasoning: The classification rests on the sole reference grammar of the language (Baird 2002 ANU thesis), which we hold as the ANU scan; the deciding passage (sec. 2.6, p.53) is confirmed verbatim on the rendered page scan, and the supporting phonotactics pages (2.4-2.5, pp.50-52: all syllables open (C)V, simple words 1-2 syllables, schwa in the vowel inventory) are also held and match the record's 'heavy'/'what counts as heavy' notes. Glottolog's bibliography has no competing grammar, phonology or sketch; Elias 2018 (the only other phonology-tagged work covering Kéo, downloaded now from Leiden, open access) takes its Kéo data from Baird and says nothing about Kéo stress. No database contradictions are recorded. Only nit: the domain-quote locator should read p.51, not p.52. engine scraping blocked), so this search of works with stress in the title for Indonesian-language skrip

tone.quote: 2.6 Stress. Stress in Indonesian languages is often a controversial issue. However, it is possible to make generalisations. Stress in Kéo is predictable: it typically falls on the penultimate syllable of the word. [...] 2.8 Intonation. There are several types of intonation contour. The choice of intonation contour is determined by a variety of factors, including the type of syntactic construction, the illocutionary force of an utterance, and the emotional state of a speaker. [...] Generally declarative sentences end in falling intonation. Interrogative sentences have rising intonation within them, typically occurring on the item that is being questioned (see §15.2).

tone.quote: Stress. Stress in Indonesian languages is a controversial issue. However, it is possible to make generalisations. Stress in Kéo falls on the penultimate syllable of the word, which is maximally disyllabic. The exception to this is in disyllabic words in which there is a schwa in the first syllable, in which case stress falls on the ultimate syllable. Stress in Indonesian loan words (such as satuju and salimu, which appear in the text below) also falls on the penultimate syllable.
